decisive_items: She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned
She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation.
There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.”
response.rationale: Prolonged daily facial triamcinolone use followed by cessation and a periorificial pustular eruption with “lakes of pus” is classic for steroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis; perioral dermatitis is too anatomically narrow, topical steroid withdrawal is a nonspecific mechanism, and contact dermatitis lacks an allergen exposure.

rejected.why: No contact allergen is identified; the eruption is temporally tied to topical steroid use and cessation rather than an exogenous contactant.
Topical steroid withdrawal is a mechanism/generic syndrome rather than the specific dermatologic diagnosis; the pustular periorificial morphology points to steroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis.
Perioral dermatitis is a related periorificial eruption, but the predominant periorbital involvement and “lakes of pus” after steroid cessation fit steroid-induced rosacea-like dermatitis better.
